questions.q: Define verbal irony and give one example from the poem where the tiger king uses verbal irony after his defeat.
questions.a: Verbal irony occurs when a speaker says the opposite of what they mean, often to mock or deceive. In the poem, the tiger king says, "We were coming to see you as friends. And that's the truth," immediately after being captured while attacking the herd — he means the opposite to manipulate Ajamil. A wrong answer (e.g., confusing verbal irony with situational irony or citing the sheep dog's silence) reveals the student cannot distinguish between irony types or locate the speaker's intent in the text.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the sheep dog's capture of 51 tigers single-handedly is an example of situational irony, and what it suggests about the relationship between power and competence in the poem's world.
questions.a: Situational irony arises when the outcome is the opposite of what is expected: the mighty tiger king leads 50 tigers expecting an easy victory, but a single sheep dog defeats them all effortlessly. This suggests that in the poem's political allegory, brute force (tigers) is incompetent against genuine competence (sheep dog), yet the system (Ajamil) rewards the former and ignores the latter. A wrong answer that only describes the event without naming "situational irony" or linking it to the poem's political message shows the student understands the plot but not the device's analytical function.

questions.q: Apply the concept of dramatic irony to the scene where Ajamil "pretended to believe every single word / of what the tiger king said." Who knows the truth that Ajamil pretends not to know, and how does this create dramatic irony for the reader?
questions.a: The sheep dog knows the truth (he "had never told a lie" and makes "frantic signs"), and the reader knows the truth from the narrative description of the attack. Ajamil pretends ignorance, creating dramatic irony because the audience understands the shepherd's complicity while the tiger king thinks he has successfully deceived him. A wrong answer that claims the tiger king is the one deceived, or that the sheep dog is fooled, reveals the student cannot track knowledge distribution among characters — a core skill for dramatic irony analysis.

questions.q: Analyze how the symbols of "the flute" and "the same pond" function together in the final stanza to represent the corrupt bargain between the political class and the oppressors at the expense of the common people.
questions.a: The flute symbolizes Ajamil's negligent leisure — he plays while his duty (protecting sheep) is abandoned. The shared pond symbolizes the false equivalence created by the treaty: tigers (predators) and sheep (prey) drinking together only because both are "well fed" on the shepherd's betrayal. Together, they represent a corrupt stability bought by sacrificing the vulnerable. A wrong answer that treats the flute as mere pastoral imagery or the pond as a peaceful scene misses the satirical edge — the student is reading literally, not symbolically.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the poem's central irony: that the shepherd signs a "friendship treaty" with the very tigers who came to eat his flock. Does this irony strengthen or weaken the poem's political satire? Justify your judgment with two textual reasons.
questions.a: The irony strengthens the satire because (1) it mirrors realpolitik where leaders legitimize threats through treaties instead of resisting them, and (2) the detail "lamb chops and the roast" served at the dinner makes the betrayal visceral — the shepherd feeds the tigers his own flock to buy peace. A wrong answer that calls the irony "confusing" or says it "weakens the message because Ajamil looks foolish" fails to recognize that the poem intends Ajamil to look complicit, not foolish — the satire targets systemic betrayal, not individual incompetence.

questions.q: Create a new two-stanza extension to the poem that uses a new symbol (not flute, pond, treaty, sheep dog) to represent the voice of the common people (sheep) reacting to the treaty. Use situational irony in your extension.
questions.a: A strong answer introduces a symbol like "a bell around the neck of the lead sheep" that rings not for grazing but for warning, yet the shepherd muffles it — situational irony because the protective device becomes a tool of silence. The extension must maintain the poem's satirical tone and four-line stanza structure. A weak answer that adds a happy ending or a revolutionary sheep dog misses the poem's bleak systemic critique — the student has not internalized the allegory's logic that the system silences dissent.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Irony in literature is a contrast between ______ and reality, where the intended meaning differs from the literal meaning, often to critique a situation; symbolism is the use of concrete objects, characters, or actions to represent abstract ideas, qualities, or societal forces beyond their literal sense.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are watching a ______ debate where a leader claims to protect the poor but passes laws that benefit only the wealthy — that gap between words and action is irony.
What is Irony in literature? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Irony in literature is a contrast between expectation and reality, where the intended meaning differs from the literal meaning, often to critique a situation; symbolism is the use of concrete objects, characters, or actions to represent abstract ideas, qualities, or societal forces beyond their literal sense.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify specific instances of verbal, situational, and dramatic irony in the poem, explain how the symbols of tigers, sheep, sheep dog, and Ajamil function as an integrated allegorical system, and write a structured analytical paragraph using the PEEL method that connects a device to the poem's satirical theme.
